posts.headline: Chief Technology Officer @ Biddano | Technology Management, Technology Leadership
posts.text: These days, building a software product has become fast, but building it right is a much bigger challenge.While building one of my products, I was bombarded with information from my AI agent. At that point, I had two options: blindly accept its suggestions or take the time to understand the information not just the code. I believe this ability will become a key hiring criterion: processing large amounts of information, applying judgment, and using that context to solve real-world problems. This is where strong analytical thinking will matter.Future interviews may focus less on DSA and more on your ability to understand complex context and make sound decisions. Those who master this skill will have a significant advantage in the tech industry. But how do you master it? From my experience, engineers now need domain expertise alongside technical skills. Engineers need to understand the broader business problem instead of thinking only at the API level. Memorising API endpoints and payloads adds little value. What matters is understanding the use cases and functionality of each API and module. You also need a strong mental model of the database structure and the relationships between its entities. When AI asks you to accept or reject a change, your judgment depends on how well you understand both the system and the business.The challenge is that AI can create hundreds of database tables in 30 minutes, but understanding and validating them takes much longer. Engineers are working with a system that can generate solutions faster than they can review them, while still lacking crucial context about the actual business problem. People working in tech need to develop these skills. Otherwise, a fresher with strong contextual understanding and judgment could deliver more value than an experienced developer. Even as IITs face placement challenges today, I believe demand for top talent will rise sharply again over the next two years with significantly higher compensation. The definition of “top talent,” however, is changing.

posts.text: You may be too small to have your own internal platform team. That’s not the same as being too small for platform engineering. If you’re a small engineering team, you don’t need a platform department. You don't need a platform product manager, a portal with forty plugins, or a team maintaining abstractions nobody asked for. That would be ridiculous, and anyone pitching it to you at that size would need a very specific reason that explains why. The question I'd ask instead is what your engineers keep doing repeatedly that you could solve once. That answer is usually concrete. Every team writing CI pipelines from scratch. The same infrastructure provisioned slightly differently each time. Setting up a test VM or DB or Cluster and spinning it down after testing. Operations that depend on one person's memory or knowledge. Everyone, including software developers, needing to know the same handful of Terraform or Kubernetes commands. Outdated Knowledge Based in Confluence. None of that needs a department. It needs a few reusable capabilities and someone who owns them. And it is very possible I once consulted for a startup where I was the only DevOps engineer supporting more than 20 engineers. No platform team. Still a platform. Automated paths and self-service, built so developers could handle their own operations without coming to me. If your engineers can already deploy, provision what they need and understand their own services without waiting on anyone, don’t build a platform because someone told you to. You’re fine. But as the product grows, so does the platform underneath it, and more of this becomes necessary. That still doesn’t mean hiring a team. The goal is to remove enough repeated work that you don’t need one yet. Which of those is costing your engineers the most time right now? #PlatformEngineering #DevOps #EngineeringLeadership

posts.text: AI just moved from “interesting tool” to “institutional priority.” In one week, we saw government rebrand AI in legal contexts as “super intelligence,” OpenAI publish math benchmark progress that’s shaking up parts of research, universities launch new AI degrees, healthcare pilots expand AI prescribing, and companies keep redirecting budgets from headcount to automation. Why this matters: For engineers and technical professionals, this is no longer just about model capabilities. It’s about how AI is being embedded into law, education, medicine, hiring, and capital allocation. The technical stack is becoming organizational strategy. 3 key takeaways: • AI is becoming a systems-level decision, not a side project The White House and DOJ signals suggest AI is being framed not just as software, but as a national capability with legal and policy implications. That changes procurement, governance, and the expectations placed on technical teams. • Frontier model progress is getting more domain-specific and harder to ignore OpenAI’s math results are drawing attention because mathematics is a proxy for reasoning, abstraction, and research assistance. Whether or not you buy the hype, engineers should expect stronger AI support in formal problem-solving, coding, verification, and scientific workflows. • The labor market is being reshaped unevenly Georgia Tech launching an online AI master’s reflects rising demand for AI skills. At the same time, Reuters reports companies are cutting jobs as investment shifts toward AI. The signal is clear: teams that can integrate, evaluate, and govern AI will likely gain leverage; teams that can’t may face compression. The bigger pattern: AI adoption is no longer constrained by model availability. It’s constrained by trust, safety guarantees, regulation, and whether organizations can turn prototypes into reliable production systems. Question for the audience: What will matter most over the next 2 years for technical professionals: • Building with AI • Evaluating and governing AI • Deep domain expertise that AI can augment • Something else entirely?

posts.text: 📌 The biggest hiring mistakes companies make aren’t always about finding the wrong candidate. Sometimes, they lose the right candidate before the hiring process even gets started. Here are 7 mistakes I keep noticing in recruitment: ❌ 1. Writing unclear job descriptions If candidates can't understand the role, responsibilities, or expectations, good candidates may simply move on. ❌ 2. Looking for a “perfect” candidate A candidate doesn't need to match 100% of the JD to become a great employee. ❌ 3. Taking too long to make decisions Good candidates usually have multiple opportunities. A slow hiring process can make companies lose them. ❌ 4. Focusing too much on degrees A qualification can show knowledge. Skills, problem-solving and adaptability show what someone can actually do. ❌ 5. Ignoring candidate experience Candidates remember how a company treats them — even when they don't get selected. ❌ 6. Using the same hiring strategy for every role Hiring a recruiter, software developer, sales professional and supply-chain analyst requires different approaches. ❌ 7. Forgetting that hiring is a two-way decision The company evaluates the candidate. But the candidate is also evaluating the company. Hiring isn't just about asking: “Is this person right for us?” It's also about asking: “Are we creating a process where the right person wants to join us?” It's about matching people, skills, expectations and business needs. #HumanResources #Recruitment #TalentAcquisition #Hiring #HR #FutureOfWork #CareerDevelopment #RecruitmentTips #Leadership #WorkplaceCulture Based on this concept give a cute proper professional image Proper seo

posts.text: 🌍 BE/B.Tech CSE Done. Should You Consider Studying Abroad? For a CSE graduate, studying abroad can be more than earning another degree. It can be an opportunity to gain global tech exposure, deeper specialization, research experience and a different way of solving engineering problems. Universities across the USA, UK, Germany, Canada, Australia, Singapore and other technology hubs offer postgraduate programs in areas such as AI/ML, Cloud Computing, Cybersecurity, Robotics, Data Science and Software Engineering. 💻 What can you gain? 🔹 Specialization — Go deeper into AI, ML, Cloud, Cybersecurity, Robotics, etc. 🔹 Research Exposure — Work on advanced technologies and real research problems 🔹 Industry Projects — Apply classroom knowledge to practical challenges 🔹 Global Collaboration — Work with students and professionals from different countries 🔹 Internships & Networking — Access university career networks and industry connections 🔹 Communication Skills — Learn to work in multicultural engineering teams 🔹 Different Tech Ecosystems — Experience how companies build products at global scale 🚀 What could the path look like? BE/B.Tech CSE → MS/MTech/MSc specialization → Projects + Research → Internship → Global Tech Experience Possible specializations: 🤖 AI & Machine Learning ☁️ Cloud & Distributed Systems 🔐 Cybersecurity 📊 Data Science 💻 Software Engineering 🦾 Robotics & Autonomous Systems ⚡ Semiconductor & Systems 🌐 Product Engineering But there is an important reality: Going abroad does not automatically create a great tech career. The current international CS job market is competitive, particularly for entry-level roles, and visa/work authorization can significantly affect opportunities. Recent reporting also shows that AI is changing traditional software-development hiring. So the goal shouldn't simply be: “I want to study abroad.” It should be: “I want to become a stronger engineer with global exposure.” Build strong DSA + programming + projects + internships + communication skills before you leave. Then use the international degree to add specialization, research, industry exposure and global perspective. 🌍 A foreign university can open doors. Your skills are what help you walk through them. #CSE #ComputerScience #StudyAbroad #TechCareers #MSinCS #IT #AI #MachineLearning #CloudComputing #SoftwareEngineering #GlobalTech #EngineeringStudents #CareerGrowth

posts.text: Pakistan’s IT exports hit a record $4.6B in FY2025–26. Great news. But there’s another side developers must watch: AI is reshaping what global clients pay for. Research from the Pakistan Business Council shows the median freelance transaction fell 41% between FY2021 and FY2025, even as total freelance exports more than doubled. More work is leaving Pakistan, but typical deals are smaller. Now add AI. Global firms increasingly use AI coding agents to automate parts of software development. Some bring work in-house they once outsourced. Outsourcing isn’t disappearing—its economics are changing. For years, Pakistan’s edge was simple: good talent at lower cost. But what happens when AI reduces the human hours needed for the same output? A client who once needed 3 developers × 160 hours may now need fewer people and fewer hours. The developer isn’t less capable—billable human work has changed. Routine tasks face the most pricing pressure: Basic websites Simple CRUD apps Repetitive integrations Basic testing & bug fixes Data entry Generic content This work isn’t vanishing overnight, but margins are shrinking. There’s another risk: the junior pipeline. If firms produce more with fewer entry-level developers, how will new talent gain experience to become senior? That said, AI won’t take all jobs. New demand is emerging in: AI integration Cloud infrastructure Data engineering Cybersecurity System architecture AI-enabled products Engineers who can implement and maintain these systems in production are in demand. The market isn’t just shrinking—it’s shifting. Pakistani developers shouldn’t respond by becoming cheaper. The opportunity is to move up the value chain. I use AI daily—it makes me faster—but it doesn’t understand the client’s business, make architectural trade-offs, explain production incidents, or take the 3am call. That part of engineering is becoming more important, not less. Pakistan’s IT opportunity is growing, but selling cheaper developer hours is losing power. The next advantage will be: AI + engineering judgment + domain knowledge + ownership. What are you seeing? Are global clients hiring fewer developers, or expecting the same developers to deliver more with AI? #Pakistan #SoftwareEngineering #AI #TechCareers #FutureOfWork

posts.text: Every few years marketing decides it wants to be engineering when it grows up. In 2010 we got the growth hacker. In 2023 Clay gave us the GTM engineer. And this April, Profound's co-founder put "marketing engineer" on a slide at his own company's conference, and at least one guy in the audience updated his LinkedIn title before the keynote was over. Respect, honestly. Six months later the marketing engineer has a manifesto, a university course, a job board, a hackathon and a podcast. Profound made all five. Actual hires? Around 173 in the past year, according to Live Data Technologies. You could seat the entire profession at a mid-sized wedding. I'm not saying the work is fake. Marketing teams really are building agents to do competitor research and buy media, and plenty of companies are rebuilding their sites so ChatGPT stops describing them wrong. Somebody has to build and run that stuff. But I'd watch who's doing the defining. GTM engineer became a real job once people with nothing to sell started writing about it. Salary surveys, newsletters, bootcamps someone doesn't own. Growth hacker went the other way. The methods got so normal that the title stopped meaning anything, and nobody really missed it. Marketing engineer hasn't hit either point yet. Right now it belongs to one software company, and the employers hiring for it can't even agree on whether they want a developer with three years of experience or the CRM person who was already automating everything in Zapier. Our guess is this ends the way growth hacking did. In a few years every good marketer builds things, and "marketing engineer" sounds about as dated as "social media guru".
